title: Statistics - Fundamentals
text:
Important



This chapter turns statistics into intuition first, formulas second. The examples are deliberately real-world and a little playful, but the definitions stay mathematically correct.

title: Statistics - Fundamentals
text:
Part 1: Foundations of Data Analysis

1. Descriptive vs. Inferential Statistics
Think of statistics as two different jobs.
Fun example first: imagine you run a cafe and record sales for 30 days.

Descriptive statistics = your monthly report card.
Inferential statistics = using those 30 days to predict next month.
Descriptive statistics summarize what you already have. It is the profile grid of your data: counts, averages, percentages, and spread.
Inferential statistics use a sample to make a claim about a larger population. It is the part where you see a few posts and try to guess the whole story.









Concept
What it does
Real-life example




Descriptive
Summarizes observed data
Average likes on your last 20 posts


Inferential
Generalizes from sample to population
Predicting how all users might behave from a test group





2. Measures of Central Tendency
Central tendency tells you where the center of the data lives.
Fun example first: five delivery times are 12, 13, 13, 14, and 45 minutes (one rider got stuck in traffic).

Mean: the arithmetic average. It is the ultimate compromise, but it is sensitive to extreme outliers.
Median: the middle value after sorting. It is much more stable when one value is wildly unusual.
Mode: the most frequent value. It is the crowd favorite.

Example: if five friends pick restaurant budgets of $20, $25, $25, $30, and $5000, the mean is dragged upward by the billionaire, while the median stays near the center.
Formula:
\[\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i\]
ML/AI use: median is often safer than mean when preprocessing skewed features.


3. Measures of Dispersion
Dispersion tells you how spread out the data is.
Fun example first: two classes can both have average score 70, but one class is tightly clustered near 70 and the other ranges from 20 to 100.

Range: the distance between the largest and smallest values.
Mean deviation: average distance from the center.
Variance and standard deviation: the core measures of spread.
Quartile deviation: focuses on the middle 50% and is less affected by outliers.

For sample data, variance is usually written as:
\[s^2 = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}\]
and standard deviation is:
\[s = \sqrt{s^2}\]
Low spread means consistency. High spread means chaos, or at least a very eventful day.
ML/AI use: standardization scales features using standard deviation.


4. Skewness and Kurtosis
Shape matters as much as center and spread.
Fun example first:

App session length is usually right-skewed (many short visits, few very long users).
Daily stock returns often have heavy tails (big surprises happen more than normal models expect).
Zero skewness: symmetric data, like a well-balanced mountain.
Positive skewness: long tail to the right. Income data is the classic example because a small number of very large values stretch the tail.
Negative skewness: long tail to the left. Early retirement ages can create this shape.
Leptokurtic: sharp peak and heavy tails. Crypto returns are a memorable example.
Platykurtic: flatter shape with lighter tails. Daily temperatures in a mild climate often feel this way.

Formulas:
\[\text{Skewness} = g_1 = \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})^3}{\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})^2\right)^{3/2}}\]
\[\text{Excess Kurtosis} = g_2 = \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})^4}{\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})^2\right)^2} - 3\]
flowchart LR
    A[Skewness = Direction of Tail] --> B[Left Tail Long = Negative Skew]
    A --> C[Balanced = Near Zero Skew]
    A --> D[Right Tail Long = Positive Skew]
ML/AI use: skewed features often benefit from log or power transforms.

title: Statistics - Fundamentals
text:
Part 2: Probability, Sampling, and Testing

5. Probability
Probability quantifies uncertainty.
Fun example first: before seeing the weather app, you estimate rain chance from the sky. After seeing dark clouds plus forecast, you update your belief.

Classical probability assumes equally likely outcomes. A fair coin has a \(1/2\) chance of landing heads.
Conditional probability updates the odds after new information arrives.

If the sky is cloudy, the chance of carrying an umbrella changes. The data is the same object, but the context is different, so the probability changes too.
Core formulas:
\[P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}\]
\[P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)\]
ML/AI use: conditional probability powers Naive Bayes classifiers.


6. Distribution and Sampling
In the real world, you usually cannot inspect every member of the population, so you sample.
Fun example first: tasting one spoon of soup is sampling; tasting every spoon is impossible.

Population: the full group you care about.
Sample: a smaller group you actually observe.
Distribution: how values are spread across the scale.

The Central Limit Theorem says that the distribution of sample means tends toward normality as sample size grows, even if the original data is messy.
\[\bar{X} \approx N\left(\mu, \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\]
That is why repeated spoonfuls of soup can reveal the flavor of the entire pot.
ML/AI use: many confidence intervals and test statistics rely on this idea.


7. Parametric vs. Non-Parametric Tests
Use the test that matches your data, not the one that looks smartest in a slide deck.
Fun example first: if shoe sizes look reasonably bell-shaped, use parametric tests; if ratings are weird and heavily skewed, rank-based tests are safer.

Parametric tests assume structure: often normality, equal variance, and other mathematical conditions. Examples include the t-test and ANOVA.
Non-parametric tests are more flexible and often rely on ranks rather than raw values. Examples include Mann-Whitney and Kruskal-Wallis.

When the data is tidy, parametric tests are powerful. When the data is messy, non-parametric tests are often safer.


8. Hypothesis Testing
Hypothesis testing asks whether an observed effect is likely real or just noise.
Fun example first: did your new landing page actually increase signups, or did you get lucky this week?

Null hypothesis (\(H_0\)): no effect, no change, no difference.
Alternative hypothesis (\(H_1\)): there is an effect.
p-value: how surprising the observed result would be if \(H_0\) were true.

Important reviewer note: a p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true. It is a probability under the assumption that the null is true.
If the p-value is small enough for your chosen threshold, you reject the null and move forward with the stronger claim.
Common test statistic:
\[z = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}\]
ML/AI use: A/B tests in product analytics are hypothesis tests.


9. Type I and Type II Errors
Even good tests can make mistakes.
Fun example first: spam filters.

Marking a good email as spam is a Type I error.
Missing a spam email is a Type II error.
Type I error: false positive. You reject \(H_0\) even though it is actually true.
Type II error: false negative. You fail to reject \(H_0\) even though it is false.

Smoke alarms are the perfect metaphor: one false alarm is annoying, but ignoring a real fire is much worse.
Power reminder:
\[\text{Power} = 1 - \beta\]
ML/AI use: threshold tuning is essentially balancing these errors.


10. ANOVA
If you want to compare more than two group means, ANOVA is the right tool.
Fun example first: three ad creatives, one budget, one KPI. ANOVA checks if at least one creative truly performs differently.
Instead of running many t-tests and inflating error risk, ANOVA compares:

variation between groups
variation within groups

The big question is simple: is at least one group genuinely different?
Example: if you test four diet plans at once, ANOVA tells you whether one of them stands out without turning the analysis into a pile of pairwise comparisons.
Formula:
\[F = \frac{\text{MS}_{\text{between}}}{\text{MS}_{\text{within}}}\]
ML/AI use: quick feature screening across multiple group labels.


11. Chi-Square Test
Chi-square is for categorical data.
Fun example first: are subscription tiers independent of preferred device type (mobile, desktop, tablet)?

Chi-square test of independence checks whether two categorical variables are related.
Chi-square goodness-of-fit checks whether observed category counts match an expected pattern.

Example: does relationship status depend on zodiac sign, or are the categories unrelated? Chi-square answers that with counts, not averages.
Formula:
\[\chi^2 = \sum \frac{(O - E)^2}{E}\]
ML/AI use: feature-label association checks for categorical variables.

title: Statistics - Fundamentals
text:
Part 3: Correlation, Regression, and Modeling

12. Correlation and Regression
Fun example first: ice cream sales and temperature rise together, but temperature is the hidden driver.

Correlation measures strength and direction of association, from \(-1\) to \(+1\).
Regression builds an equation to predict one variable from another.

Positive correlation means two variables move together. Negative correlation means one rises while the other falls. Zero correlation means there is no linear relationship.
Reviewer note: correlation is not causation. Two variables can move together because of a hidden third factor, coincidence, or shared trend.
Key formulas:
\[r = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sqrt{\sum (x_i-\bar{x})^2\sum (y_i-\bar{y})^2}}\]
\[\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\]
ML/AI use: correlation heatmaps help detect redundant features.


13. Correlation Types for Real Data
Fun example first: leaderboard ranks are not evenly spaced numbers, so rank correlation is often better than Pearson.

Pearson: linear relationship on numeric values.
Spearman: monotonic relationship on ranks.
Kendall: rank agreement strength, robust for small samples.

Quick rule:

Use Pearson for roughly linear, continuous features.
Use Spearman/Kendall when outliers or nonlinearity make raw values unreliable.

ML/AI use: Spearman is common in feature engineering sanity checks.


14. Regression Assumptions
Linear regression works best when its assumptions are respected.

Linearity: the relationship should be roughly straight.
Independence of errors: one residual should not predict the next.
Homoscedasticity: the error spread should stay roughly constant.
Normality of residuals: the errors should look approximately normal.

If the fit is a highway, the road should not turn into a rollercoaster with widening lanes and echoing bumps.
Residual idea:
\[e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i\]
ML/AI use: residual diagnostics catch model misspecification early.


15. Data Transformation for Regression
Sometimes a transform makes the pattern visible.
Fun example first: if influencer follower counts range from 200 to 20 million, raw scale hides useful patterns.

Log transform: compresses large values and reduces skew.
Square root transform: useful for moderate right-skew.
Power transform: stretches or compresses the scale to improve linearity.

Example: log-transforming income can make the difference between regular salaries and billionaire wealth easier to model.
Formula:
\[x' = \log(x + c)\]


16. Dummy Variables
Regression wants numbers, so categorical variables need encoding.
Fun example first: for color = {red, blue, green}, do not feed words directly to linear models.

Use 1 for presence of a category.
Use 0 for absence.
Drop one reference category to avoid perfect multicollinearity.

If you have VIP, VVIP, and General membership, you only need two dummy variables. The omitted category becomes the baseline.


17. Variable Selection
Not every available feature deserves a seat in the model.
Fun example first: packing for travel with one small bag forces you to keep only useful items.

Forward selection starts small and adds useful variables.
Backward elimination starts large and removes weak variables.
Stepwise selection adds and removes variables as it goes.

Think of it like packing for a trip: the goal is to bring the essentials, not the entire closet.
ML/AI use: combine statistical selection with cross-validation, not p-values alone.


18. Logistic Regression
When the outcome is binary, logistic regression is the right fit.
Fun example first: will a customer churn this month: yes or no?
It converts a linear score into a probability using the sigmoid curve:
\[p = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}\]
Example: should a user buy or not buy, click or not click, stay or leave? Logistic regression gives a probability, then a threshold turns that probability into a class.
Log-odds form:
\[\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \cdots + \beta_kx_k\]

title: Statistics - Fundamentals
section: Part 4: Classification, Clustering, and Time Series
text:
Part 4: Classification, Clustering, and Time Series

19. Discriminant Analysis
Discriminant analysis separates known classes using the features that best distinguish them.
The Sorting Hat metaphor works well here: you already know the possible houses, and the model helps decide where a new person belongs.


20. Cluster Analysis
Cluster analysis finds natural groupings when the data has no labels.
Fun example first: at a food festival, people naturally gather by cuisine preference.
Example: people at a music festival cluster into different crowds based on taste, dress, and behavior. The algorithm groups similar points together using distance or similarity.
K-means objective:
\[\min \sum_{j=1}^{k}\sum_{x_i \in C_j} ||x_i - \mu_j||^2\]
ML/AI use: customer segmentation, anomaly pre-grouping, and recommendation bootstrapping.


21. Time Series and Forecasting
Time series data has order, not just values.
Fun example first: coffee sales peak every Monday morning and dip on Sundays.

Trend: long-term direction.
Seasonality: repeating calendar pattern.
Cyclical: longer waves without fixed timing.
Noise: the random part.

Example: winter coats spike every December, but an unexpected supply shock or pandemic can create irregular movement on top of the usual pattern.
Simple additive model:
\[Y_t = T_t + S_t + C_t + E_t\]


22. Model Evaluation
Once you build a model, you need to score it properly.
Fun example first: a medical test that predicts “healthy” for everyone can still look good on raw accuracy if disease is rare.

Confusion matrix: TP, TN, FP, FN.
Accuracy: overall correctness.
Precision: how many predicted positives were actually positive.
Recall: how many actual positives were found.
F1-score: balance between precision and recall.
ROC-AUC: how well the model ranks positives above negatives across thresholds.

If a disease screening model predicts “healthy” for almost everyone, accuracy can look excellent while the model still fails the people who need help. That is why precision, recall, and AUC matter.
Formulas:
\[\text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP+FP}\]
\[\text{Recall} = \frac{TP}{TP+FN}\]
\[F_1 = 2\cdot\frac{\text{Precision}\cdot\text{Recall}}{\text{Precision}+\text{Recall}}\]
flowchart LR
    A[Predicted Positive] --> B[True Positive]
    A --> C[False Positive]
    D[Predicted Negative] --> E[True Negative]
    D --> F[False Negative]

title: Statistics - Fundamentals
section: Part 5: Fun Statistical Methods for ML and AI
text:
Part 5: Fun Statistical Methods for ML and AI

23. Bayes Theorem and Naive Bayes
Fun example first: a movie recommender updates your “will like sci-fi” probability after seeing you watched three space movies this week.
Bayes theorem:
\[P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(B\mid A)P(A)}{P(B)}\]
Naive Bayes assumes features are conditionally independent given the class.
ML/AI use: text classification, spam detection, baseline classifiers.


24. Confidence Intervals
Fun example first: your app conversion is 8%, but the interval says true performance likely sits between 7.2% and 8.8%.
95% CI for a mean (large sample):
\[\bar{x} \pm z_{0.975}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\]
ML/AI use: report uncertainty, not just point estimates.


25. Bootstrapping
Fun example first: you repeatedly refill a sample bag from itself to see how stable your metric is.
Process:

Sample with replacement from data.
Compute metric each time.
Use the distribution of metrics for intervals.

ML/AI use: robust uncertainty when analytic formulas are hard.


26. Cross-Validation
Fun example first: instead of judging a singer from one performance, you judge across many stages.
In \(k\)-fold CV, split data into \(k\) parts, train on \(k-1\) parts, validate on the remaining part, repeat.
\[\text{CV Error} = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k} \text{Error}_i\]
flowchart TD
    A[Dataset] --> B[Split into k folds]
    B --> C[Train on k-1 folds]
    B --> D[Validate on 1 fold]
    C --> E[Repeat k times]
    D --> E
    E --> F[Average score]
ML/AI use: better estimate of out-of-sample performance.


27. Bias-Variance Tradeoff
Fun example first: a model can be too simple (misses patterns) or too complex (memorizes noise).

High bias: underfitting.
High variance: overfitting.
Goal: balanced generalization.

Decomposition idea:
\[\text{Expected Error} \approx \text{Bias}^2 + \text{Variance} + \text{Noise}\]
ML/AI use: controls model complexity and regularization strategy.


28. Regularization (L1 and L2)
Fun example first: adding luggage fees forces you to pack only what matters.

L1 (Lasso) can shrink some coefficients to exactly zero.
L2 (Ridge) shrinks coefficients smoothly.

Formulas:
\[\text{Lasso: } \min \sum (y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2 + \lambda\sum |\beta_j|\]
\[\text{Ridge: } \min \sum (y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2 + \lambda\sum \beta_j^2\]
ML/AI use: combats overfitting and improves stability.


29. Entropy and Information Gain
Fun example first: a good yes/no question in a guessing game cuts uncertainty fast.
Entropy:
\[H(S) = -\sum_i p_i\log_2 p_i\]
Information gain:
\[IG = H(\text{parent}) - \sum_v \frac{|S_v|}{|S|}H(S_v)\]
ML/AI use: decision trees choose splits with high information gain.


30. PCA (Principal Component Analysis)
Fun example first: if you photograph a 3D object from the best angle, you still keep most shape information in 2D.
PCA finds directions (principal components) with maximum variance.
Optimization view:
\[\max_{\|w\|=1} \; w^T\Sigma w\]
ML/AI use: dimensionality reduction, visualization, denoising.


31. Outlier Detection with Z-Score and IQR
Fun example first: if one user clicks 10,000 times in a minute, that point deserves investigation.
Z-score:
\[z = \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\]
IQR rule:
\[x < Q1 - 1.5\cdot IQR \quad \text{or} \quad x > Q3 + 1.5\cdot IQR\]
ML/AI use: anomaly detection and robust data cleaning.


32. Which Method Should I Use First?
flowchart TD
    A[Start with your question] --> B{Target type?}
    B -->|Numeric| C[Regression / ANOVA / Correlation]
    B -->|Category| D[Chi-square / Logistic / Naive Bayes]
    B -->|No labels| E[Clustering / PCA]
    C --> F[Validate with CV and residual checks]
    D --> F
    E --> F






Tip



Quick reviewer rule: always ask three questions before trusting a result.

Is the data type correct for the test?
Are the assumptions reasonable?
Does the metric match the real-world cost of mistakes?

title: Statistics - Fundamentals
text:
Final Takeaway
Statistics is not just formulas. It is the discipline of asking better questions, measuring uncertainty honestly, and choosing the right tool for the data you actually have.
If you remember only one idea, remember this: describe first, infer carefully, and always check the assumptions before you trust the conclusion.
Bonus memory trick: if you are stuck, start with these four in order.

Plot the data.
Check spread and skew.
Pick a method that matches data type.
Validate with out-of-sample testing.

Welcome! This is not just code snippets. You’ll learn R the way professionals do: by understanding why we use each concept, with real-world stories, before writing a single line of code.
Whether you’re a clinical programmer, SAS expert, statistician, or complete beginner—this tutorial is designed for you.





Imagine you’re a clinical researcher with patient data from 5,000 subjects. You need to: - Clean messy data (missing values, typos, wrong formats) - Calculate statistics (mean, median, confidence intervals) - Create visualizations (plots, charts, tables) - Generate a report with all results
In SAS: You’d write 50+ lines of PROC code, manage libraries, and wait for compilation.
In R: You load a dataset, clean it, analyze it, and visualize it—all in 20 lines. The results appear instantly.
R is a language designed by statisticians FOR statisticians. It’s like having a super-smart assistant who: - Understands data intuitively - Can do complex math instantly - Creates beautiful visualizations - Scales from small datasets to millions of rows - Works on any device (Windows, Mac, Linux)

A vector is like a shopping list: - All items are groceries (same type) - Each item is separate but in the same list - You can count them, sort them, or find specific ones
Think of patient data from a clinical trial:

cholesterol <- c(210, 195, 240, 185, 220)
That’s a vector of 5 numbers.

You’re conducting a diabetes study tracking:

patients <- data.frame(
  patient_id = c(1001, 1002, 1003, 1004),
  name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie", "Diana"),
  age = c(52, 45, 58, 50),
  glucose_baseline = c(245, 198, 310, 225),
  treatment = c("Drug_A", "Drug_B", "Drug_A", "Placebo"),
  improved = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)

# View the full dataset
print(patients)

3        1003 Charlie  58              310    Drug_A     TRUE

# Get specific cell

print(avg_glucose)  # 244.5 mg/dL

trial_data <- data.frame(
  patient = c("P001", "P002", "P003"),
  medication = c("Aspirin_100mg", "Aspirin_100mg", "Placebo"),
  baseline_heart_rate = c(72, 88, 75),

# Calculate average improvement

A function is like a recipe or vending machine: - Input: Ingredients (or coins) - Process: Follow instructions (or mechanism) - Output: Result (meal or snack)



Instead of writing the same calculation 50 times:
# OLD (repetitive, error-prone)
result1 <- (value1 - min_val) / (max_val - min_val)
result2 <- (value2 - min_val) / (max_val - min_val)
result3 <- (value3 - min_val) / (max_val - min_val)
# ... repeated 50 more times!
Write it ONCE as a function:
# NEW (clean, reusable)
normalize_value <- function(value, min_val, max_val) {
  result <- (value - min_val) / (max_val - min_val)
  return(result)
}

# Now use it 50 times easily
result1 <- normalize_value(value1, 0, 100)
result2 <- normalize_value(value2, 0, 100)
result3 <- normalize_value(value3, 0, 100)



# BMI = weight (kg) / (height (m))^2
# Instead of calculating this for every patient...

calculate_bmi <- function(weight_kg, height_cm) {
  height_m <- height_cm / 100
  bmi <- weight_kg / (height_m ^ 2)
  return(bmi)
}

# Now use it for any patient
bmi_alice <- calculate_bmi(75, 170)     # 26.0
bmi_bob <- calculate_bmi(82, 175)       # 26.8
bmi_charlie <- calculate_bmi(95, 180)   # 29.3

print(bmi_alice)    # 26.0
print(bmi_bob)      # 26.8
print(bmi_charlie)  # 29.3



In clinical trials, you often use the same dosing formula:
# Default: Adult dosing
calculate_dose <- function(patient_weight, dose_per_kg = 5) {
  total_dose <- patient_weight * dose_per_kg
  return(total_dose)
}

# Adult (75 kg): standard dose is 375 mg
adult_dose <- calculate_dose(75)  # Uses default 5 mg/kg
print(adult_dose)  # 375

# Child (30 kg): might need different dose
child_dose <- calculate_dose(30, dose_per_kg = 3)  # Custom 3 mg/kg
print(child_dose)  # 90

  print("ALERT: Fever detected! Notify physician!")

  print("WARNING: Slight elevation. Monitor closely.")
} else {
  print("Normal temperature.")

age <- 52

family_history <- TRUE

  risk <- "High"
} else if (fasting_glucose > 150) {
  risk <- "Moderate"
} else {
  risk <- "Low"
}

# Output: "Risk level: High"

test_result <- 8.5  # Hemoglobin g/dL

if (test_result < 7) {
  severity <- "Critical"
} else if (test_result < 8) {
  severity <- "Severe"
} else if (test_result < 10) {
  severity <- "Moderate"
} else if (test_result < 12) {
  severity <- "Mild"
} else {
  severity <- "Normal"
}

# OR use switch with intervals:
get_severity <- function(hgb) {
  if (hgb < 7) return("Critical")
  if (hgb < 8) return("Severe")
  if (hgb < 10) return("Moderate")
  if (hgb < 12) return("Mild")
  return("Normal")
}

print(get_severity(8.5))  # "Moderate"







A loop is like reading a checklist: - “Check blood pressure for patient 1” - “Check blood pressure for patient 2” - …repeat for all 100 patients



You need to check 5 patients’ lab results:
# WITHOUT loop (tedious)
glucose_1 <- 245
status_1 <- if (glucose_1 > 200) "At Risk" else "Normal"

glucose_2 <- 198
status_2 <- if (glucose_2 > 200) "At Risk" else "Normal"

glucose_3 <- 310
status_3 <- if (glucose_3 > 200) "At Risk" else "Normal"
# ... repeat 47 more times for 50 patients!

# WITH loop (clean)
glucose_readings <- c(245, 198, 310, 185, 225)

for (glucose in glucose_readings) {
  if (glucose > 200) {
    print(paste("Glucose:", glucose, "→ AT RISK"))
  } else {
    print(paste("Glucose:", glucose, "→ Normal"))
  }
}

# Output:
# Glucose: 245 → AT RISK
# Glucose: 198 → Normal
# Glucose: 310 → AT RISK
# Glucose: 185 → Normal
# Glucose: 225 → AT RISK



# Check all patients in a clinical trial
trial <- data.frame(
  patient = c("P001", "P002", "P003"),
  bmi = c(24.5, 32.1, 26.8)
)

for (i in 1:nrow(trial)) {
  patient_id <- trial[i, "patient"]
  bmi_value <- trial[i, "bmi"]
  
  if (bmi_value > 30) {
    print(paste(patient_id, "is obese (BMI =", bmi_value, ")"))
  } else {

  }

# Output:

# P002 is obese (BMI = 32.1 )
# P003 is normal (BMI = 26.8 )







Clinical data often includes notes, diagnoses, and comments. R can: - Combine text (concatenate) - Extract parts of text - Search for patterns - Replace words



first_name <- "John"
last_name <- "Smith"
diagnosis <- "Type 2 Diabetes"

# Combine text
full_note <- paste(first_name, last_name, "diagnosed with", diagnosis)
print(full_note)
# Output: "John Smith diagnosed with Type 2 Diabetes"

# Extract parts
text <- "Patient: John Smith, Age: 52, Diagnosis: HTN"
name_part <- substr(text, 9, 19)  # Extract "John Smith"
print(name_part)

# Replace text
original <- "The patient has diabtes"  # Typo
corrected <- gsub("diabtes", "diabetes", original)
print(corrected)
# Output: "The patient has diabetes"



# Lab report text
report <- "WBC: 7.5 K/uL, Hemoglobin: 14.2 g/dL, Platelets: 250 K/uL"

# Check if abnormal values are mentioned
is_normal <- !grepl("abnormal|low|high", report, ignore.case=TRUE)
print(is_normal)  # TRUE (no abnormal values flagged)

# Count number of tests
num_tests <- length(strsplit(report, ",")[[1]])
print(num_tests)  # 3 tests reported

# Patient enrolled on January 15, 2024
# Follow-up scheduled 30 days later
enroll_date <- as.Date("2024-01-15")
followup_date <- enroll_date + 30

print(followup_date)  # 2024-02-14

# How many days between events?

# Is follow-up overdue? (scheduled for 35 days)

visits <- data.frame(
  visit_date = as.Date(c("2024-01-15", "2024-02-14", "2024-04-15")),
  visit_type = c("Baseline", "Week 4", "Week 12"),
  glucose = c(245, 215, 185)

# Show visit dates nicely
for (i in 1:nrow(visits)) {
  date_str <- format(visits[i, "visit_date"], "%B %d, %Y")  # "January 15, 2024"
  print(paste(visits[i, "visit_type"], "→", date_str))
}







Loops are slow. R has a faster way called “apply family”:
# SLOW approach (loop)
numbers <- 1:10
squared <- c()
for (i in numbers) {
  squared <- c(squared, i^2)
}

# FAST approach (vectorized)
squared <- numbers^2  # R does all 10 at once!

# PROFESSIONAL approach (apply family)
squared <- sapply(numbers, function(x) x^2)



# 10 patients need weight-based dosing (5 mg/kg)
patient_weights <- c(75, 82, 68, 95, 70, 88, 65, 92, 78, 85)

# Calculate dose for each using sapply
doses <- sapply(patient_weights, function(w) w * 5)
print(doses)
# Output: 375 410 340 475 350 440 325 460 390 425



# lapply returns a list
results <- lapply(c(2, 3, 4), function(x) x^2)

# tapply groups by category
glucose <- c(245, 198, 310, 185, 225, 200)
group <- c("Drug_A", "Drug_B", "Drug_A", "Drug_B", "Drug_A", "Drug_B")
avg_by_group <- tapply(glucose, group, mean)
# Drug_A: 260, Drug_B: 191.67







A matrix is a rectangular grid of numbers (like a spreadsheet with only numbers).



# Lab values for 4 patients
patient_data <- matrix(
  c(
    245, 185, 65,      # Patient 1: glucose, LDL, HDL
    198, 210, 55,      # Patient 2
    310, 240, 48,      # Patient 3
    225, 195, 60       # Patient 4
  ),
  nrow = 4,
  ncol = 3,
  byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(
    c("P001", "P002", "P003", "P004"),
    c("Glucose", "LDL", "HDL")
  )
)

print(patient_data)

# Calculate average for each column
col_means <- apply(patient_data, 2, mean)
print(col_means)
# Glucose: 244.5, LDL: 207.5, HDL: 57

text:
A function is like a recipe or vending machine: - Input: Ingredients (or coins) - Process: Follow instructions (or mechanism) - Output: Result (meal or snack)



Instead of writing the same calculation 50 times:
# OLD (repetitive, error-prone)
result1 <- (value1 - min_val) / (max_val - min_val)
result2 <- (value2 - min_val) / (max_val - min_val)
result3 <- (value3 - min_val) / (max_val - min_val)
# ... repeated 50 more times!
Write it ONCE as a function:
# NEW (clean, reusable)
normalize_value <- function(value, min_val, max_val) {
  result <- (value - min_val) / (max_val - min_val)
  return(result)
}

# Now use it 50 times easily
result1 <- normalize_value(value1, 0, 100)
result2 <- normalize_value(value2, 0, 100)
result3 <- normalize_value(value3, 0, 100)



# BMI = weight (kg) / (height (m))^2
# Instead of calculating this for every patient...

calculate_bmi <- function(weight_kg, height_cm) {
  height_m <- height_cm / 100
  bmi <- weight_kg / (height_m ^ 2)
  return(bmi)
}

# Now use it for any patient
bmi_alice <- calculate_bmi(75, 170)     # 26.0
bmi_bob <- calculate_bmi(82, 175)       # 26.8
bmi_charlie <- calculate_bmi(95, 180)   # 29.3

print(bmi_alice)    # 26.0
print(bmi_bob)      # 26.8
print(bmi_charlie)  # 29.3



In clinical trials, you often use the same dosing formula:
# Default: Adult dosing
calculate_dose <- function(patient_weight, dose_per_kg = 5) {
  total_dose <- patient_weight * dose_per_kg
  return(total_dose)
}

# Adult (75 kg): standard dose is 375 mg
adult_dose <- calculate_dose(75)  # Uses default 5 mg/kg
print(adult_dose)  # 375

# Child (30 kg): might need different dose
child_dose <- calculate_dose(30, dose_per_kg = 3)  # Custom 3 mg/kg
print(child_dose)  # 90

title: Docker — Professional Tutorial for Life Sciences
text:
1. Introduction
Docker is a platform that packages an application and everything it needs to run — code, libraries, settings — into a portable unit called a container.

Why Docker exists
Before containers, teams struggled with a familiar problem: “It works on my machine.” Different laptops, servers, and cloud environments had different software versions. Results changed. Audits failed. Pipelines broke in production.
Docker was created to make software portable, repeatable, and isolated.


The problem Docker solves








Problem
Without Docker
With Docker




Environment differences
Results vary by machine
Same image → same behavior


Complex installs
Days installing bioinformatics tools
Pull a pre-built image in minutes


Reproducibility
Hard to prove what ran
Versioned images document the environment


Isolation
Tools conflict on one server
Each container runs independently





Where Docker is used in industry

Pharmaceutical R&D — reproducible ML and cheminformatics environments
Clinical programming — fixed R/SAS/Python stacks for TLF generation
Bioinformatics — pipelines for genomics, proteomics, and multi-omics
Healthcare AI — deploying models in controlled containers
Cloud & DevOps — AWS ECS, Google Cloud Run, Kubernetes workloads







Tip



Beginner takeaway: Docker is a standardized box for software. Same box, same result — on your laptop, a lab server, or the cloud.

Explain what Docker is and why regulated industries use it

3. Why is this important?

Why should someone learn Docker?
Docker is one of the most requested skills in bioinformatics, data engineering, and DevOps job postings. It turns fragile setups into shareable, testable environments.


Why do companies use it?

Speed — onboard new analysts in hours, not weeks
Compliance — versioned images support audit trails
Scale — same container runs on one laptop or 1,000 cloud nodes
Cost — efficient resource use compared to full virtual machines



Why is it important in bioinformatics?
Genomics pipelines combine dozens of tools (FastQC, BWA, GATK, bcftools). Docker (and Biocontainers) pins exact versions so published results can be reproduced.


Why is it important in clinical programming?
Clinical trial analysis must be reproducible. Docker ensures the same R packages, SAS components, or Python libraries are used for every database lock and QC re-run.


Why is it useful in data science?
Data scientists package models with dependencies so staging and production environments match — reducing “model works locally but fails in deployment” issues.

text:
6. Basic Concepts

Image







Definition
Read-only template containing an app and its dependencies


Analogy
A sealed recipe kit with pre-measured ingredients


Industry example
rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 for a locked clinical R environment


Best practice
Always use specific version tags — never :latest in production





Container







Definition
A running instance of an image


Analogy
The actual meal cooked from the recipe kit


Industry example
One container per study analysis run


Best practice
Use --rm for temporary jobs; name containers in long-running services





Registry







Definition
Storage and distribution system for images


Analogy
A warehouse catalog of standardized boxes


Industry example
Private AWS ECR registry for validated pharma images


Best practice
Use private registries for internal and GxP workloads





Docker Hub







Definition
Public registry maintained by Docker


Analogy
An app store for container images


Industry example
Pulling official python:3.11-slim base images


Best practice
Prefer verified publishers; scan images for vulnerabilities





Dockerfile







Definition
Text file with step-by-step instructions to build an image


Analogy
The master recipe card


Industry example
Documented build file archived with study deliverables


Best practice
Keep Dockerfiles in version control; review changes like code





Volume







Definition
Persistent storage mounted into a container


Analogy
A USB drive plugged into the box


Industry example
Mount clinical CSV input and TLF output folders


Best practice
Never store patient data inside the image — mount at runtime





Network







Definition
Virtual network allowing containers to communicate


Analogy
Phone lines between offices in the same building


Industry example
Connect a Shiny app container to a PostgreSQL container


Best practice
Use custom networks; avoid exposing unnecessary ports

7. Hands-on Examples

Example 1 — Hello World
Problem: Confirm Docker is installed and working.
Solution: Run the official test image.
docker run hello-world
Expected output: Message containing Hello from Docker!
Explanation: Docker downloaded a tiny image, started a container, printed output, and exited.



Example 2 — Run R without installing R
Problem: You need R 4.3 but do not want to install it locally.
Solution:
docker run --rm rocker/r-ver:4.3 R --version
Expected output: R version 4.3.x ...
Explanation: The container includes R; your host machine stays unchanged.



Example 3 — Interactive Python shell
Problem: Test Python in an isolated environment.
Solution:
docker run -it --rm python:3.11-slim python
print("Docker Python ready")
exit()
Expected result: Python REPL opens, prints message, exits cleanly.



Example 4 — Build a clinical summary image
Problem: Create a reproducible environment for summarizing patient ages.
Solution:
Create summarize.R:
args <- commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE)
dat <- read.csv(args[1])
out <- data.frame(
  n = nrow(dat),
  mean_age = round(mean(dat$age, na.rm = TRUE), 1)
)
write.csv(out, args[2], row.names = FALSE)
cat("Done\n")
Create patients.csv:
patient_id,age
001,54
002,61
003,47
Create Dockerfile:
FROM rocker/r-ver:4.3
WORKDIR /analysis
COPY summarize.R patients.csv ./
CMD ["Rscript", "summarize.R", "patients.csv", "summary.csv"]
Build and run:
docker build -t clinical-summary:1.0 .
docker run --rm -v "$(pwd):/output" clinical-summary:1.0 \
  sh -c "Rscript summarize.R patients.csv /output/summary.csv"
cat summary.csv
Expected output: CSV with n and mean_age.
Explanation: Image tag clinical-summary:1.0 documents the exact environment used.



Example 5 — Pull a bioinformatics tool
Problem: Run FastQC without manual installation.
Solution:
docker run --rm biocontainers/fastqc:v0.11.9_cv8 fastqc --help
Expected result: FastQC help text displayed.

A: An image is a read-only template; a container is a running instance of that image.
Q2: What is Docker Hub?
A: A public registry for storing and sharing container images.
Q3: Why do bioinformatics teams use Docker?
A: To pin tool versions and reproduce pipeline results across machines.


Intermediate
Q4: What is a volume and when would you use one?
A: Persistent storage mounted into a container — used for input data and output results without baking them into the image.
Q5: How do Docker and Kubernetes relate?
A: Docker builds/runs containers locally; Kubernetes orchestrates many containers across a cluster.
Q6: How would you make a clinical analysis reproducible with Docker?
A: Build a versioned image, document the tag/digest, mount study data at runtime, archive the Dockerfile in version control.


Advanced
Q7: What are multi-stage builds?
A: Dockerfiles with multiple FROM stages — compile in one stage, copy only artifacts to a smaller final image.
Q8: How do you reduce attack surface in production containers?
A: Non-root user, minimal base image, no secrets in layers, regular scanning, read-only filesystem where possible.
Q9: Explain how Nextflow uses Docker.
A: Each process specifies a container image; Nextflow pulls and runs it per task, enabling reproducible scalable pipelines.

6. Basic Concepts

Process







Definition
A single computational step with inputs, outputs, and a script


Analogy
One station on a factory assembly line


Industry example
FastQC on each FASTQ file in parallel


Best practice
One logical task per process; pin container versions





Channel







Definition
An asynchronous queue connecting processes with data


Analogy
A conveyor belt carrying work items


Industry example
One channel item per patient sample


Best practice
Use tuple channels for paired-end reads





Workflow







Definition
The DAG (graph) linking processes


Analogy
The master floor plan of the factory


Industry example
QC → align → call variants → annotate


Best practice
Keep main.nf readable; modularize with include





Executor







Definition
Backend that runs tasks (local, slurm, awsbatch, etc.)


Analogy
The HR department assigning workers to stations


Industry example
awsbatch for cloud scale


Best practice
Use profiles in nextflow.config





Profile







Definition
Named configuration bundle (executor, containers, paths)


Analogy
A preset mode: “laptop” vs “cloud”


Industry example
-profile docker,aws


Best practice
Never hardcode credentials in profiles





Container directive



Definition
Docker/Singularity image used by a process


Analogy
The standardized toolbox for that station


Industry example
biocontainers/fastqc:v0.11.9_cv8


Best practice
Always specify full image tags





work/ directory



Definition
Cached task directories for resume and debugging


Analogy
The workshop floor where in-progress jobs live


Industry example
Inspected when a variant-calling step fails


Best practice
Use shared workDir on cloud; enable -resume

7. Hands-on Examples

Example 1 — Hello World
Problem: Verify Nextflow runs locally.
Solution: Create main.nf:
#!/usr/bin/env nextflow

process sayHello {
  output:
    path 'hello.txt'

  script:
  """
  echo "Hello from Nextflow" > hello.txt
  """
}

workflow {
  sayHello()
}
Run:
nextflow run main.nf
cat work/*/hello.txt
Expected output: Hello from Nextflow



Example 2 — Parallel sample processing
Problem: Process multiple samples in parallel.
Solution:
params.samples = ['S1', 'S2', 'S3']

process greetSample {
  input:
    val sample

  output:
    stdout

  script:
  """
  echo "Processing sample ${sample}"
  """
}

workflow {
  Channel.fromList(params.samples) | greetSample | view
}
Expected result: Three lines, order may vary (parallel execution).



Example 3 — Dockerized FastQC
Problem: Run FastQC in a reproducible container.
Solution:
process runFastqc {
  container 'biocontainers/fastqc:v0.11.9_cv8'

  input:
    path fastq

  output:
    path "*.html"

  script:
  """
  fastqc ${fastq}
  """
}

workflow {
  Channel.fromPath('*.fastq.gz') | runFastqc
}
Expected result: HTML QC reports per FASTQ file.



Example 4 — Python in Nextflow
Problem: Run a Python script inside a pipeline.
Solution:
process runPython {
  container 'python:3.11-slim'

  input:
    path csv

  output:
    path 'out.txt'

  script:
  """
  python -c "import pandas as pd; df=pd.read_csv('${csv}'); print(df.shape)" > out.txt
  """
}



Example 5 — R analysis step
Problem: Execute analysis.R with Dockerized R.
Solution:
process runR {
  container 'rocker/r-ver:4.3'

  input:
    path input_csv

  output:
    path 'output.csv'

  script:
  """
  Rscript analysis.R ${input_csv} output.csv
  """
}
analysis.R:
args <- commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE)
dat <- read.csv(args[1])
